newsitem.title: USA: Deere sees higher physical sales volume.
newsitem.headline: Deere sees higher physical sales volume.

text.p: Deere & Co said Tuesday it expects physical volume of sales to dealers to rise eight percent in 1997 from year-ago levels, a higher projection than the six percent increase it had previously expected.
Deere, which makes agricultural and construction equipment, also said it expected third quarter comparable physical volume of sales to dealers will be up 10 percent from year-ago levels.
Deere said the third quarter outlook is higher than previously planned. A spokesman said the previous third-quarter projection had not been public.

"Overall, the outlook for the company's businesses remains very positive," Hans Becherer, chairman, said. "Although we are investing in numerous strategic growth opportunities throughout the world, our overall net sales and revenues and operating margins continue at strong levels due to favorable market conditions and our continuous improvement initiatives."

Deere reported earnings for the second quarter ended April 30 of $1.25 a share, up from $1.04 a year ago. Revenues for the quarter rose 14 percent to $3.52 billion. Six-month earnings were $1.94 a share on sales of $5.92 billion, up from year-ago earnings of $1.67 on sales of $5.41 billion.

"The company's strong results for the first six months were in line with our expectations for both the period and the full year," Becherer said in a statement. "The remainder of 1997 should benefit from a growing global economy, healthy agricultural markets and generally higher levels of farmer confidence."

He added that improving dietary trends and rapid income growth in many developing nations continue to stimulate strong demand for farm commodities, and grain and oilseed prices remain at relatively strong levels.

"Additionally, in 1996, many U.S. farmers received substantial direct government payments provided by the new farm bill and these payments, which were unrelated to commodity prices, are expected to continue during 1996," Becherer said.
Based on these factors, he said the company expects another strong year in 1997 for Deere's agricultural equipment division.

"Industry retail demand for construction equipment is strong and is expected to remain at similar levels throughout 1997 as favorable economic growth, rising incomes and low inflation rates continue to result in good housing demand," Becherer said.
He added that Deere retail demand is expected to benefit from sales of recently announced new construction equipment models.

"In summary, industry demand for our products remains strong, and the recent introductions of a wide array of exciting new products should promote market share growth in existing and new markets throughout the world," Becherer said. "Based on these factors, we expect continued excellent operating performance during the remainder of 1997."
